promise: After this you can explain what a Bloom filter, a HyperLogLog and a count-min sketch do, what error each one makes, and follow the two Meta posts on the topic page.

terms.definition: A function that turns any input into a fixed-size number that looks random and is always the same for the same input.
A row of positions that each hold 0 or 1.
How many different items there are, counting each one once however often it appears.

before.note: Read Storage Engines first: it shows the LSM-tree read path where Bloom filters earn their place. Nothing else is assumed; the hashing and probability on this page are explained from the start.

stages.name: Basics
body: Some questions are too expensive to answer exactly, so these structures answer approximately from a small, fixed amount of memory. The Redis documentation puts the trade plainly for the Bloom filter: it stores hashed representations of the items instead of the items, so it gives up some precision and gains space and speed [[redis-bloom]].

A Bloom filter can guarantee that an item is absent from a set but can only estimate that it is present. A negative answer is certain, and one in N positive answers will be wrong [[redis-bloom]]. RocksDB uses the same wording: given a key, the filter says the key may exist or definitely does not exist [[rocks-bloom]].

That asymmetry is what makes the filter a guard. Redis lists checking whether a username is taken as a use: if the filter says no, the name is free, and if it says yes the app can check the main database [[redis-bloom]]. RocksDB puts a filter in every new sorted file when a filter policy is set, to decide whether the file may contain the key [[rocks-bloom]].

terms.definition: A compact structure that gives an answer with a bounded chance of error instead of an exact answer.
A bit array that says a key is definitely absent or may be present.
A "may be present" answer for a key that was never added.
An "absent" answer for a key that was added. A Bloom filter never gives one.

stages.name: How it works
body: RocksDB describes the mechanism: several hash functions are applied to a key, each picking a bit to set to 1. At read time the same hash functions are applied to the search key and the bits are probed. If at least one probe returns 0, the key definitely does not exist [[rocks-bloom]].

Redis gives the sizing arithmetic. The optimal number of hash functions is ceil(-ln(error_rate) / ln(2)), and the bits per item are -ln(error_rate) / ln(2)^2. A 1% error rate needs 7 hash functions and 9.585 bits per item; 0.1% needs 10 and 14.378; 0.01% needs 14 and 19.170 [[redis-bloom]]. The page contrasts this with a Redis set holding IP addresses, at around 40 bytes (320 bits) per item [[redis-bloom]].

Counting distinct items works differently. Redis describes a HyperLogLog as a probabilistic structure that estimates the cardinality of a set. PFADD adds elements, PFCOUNT returns the approximate count, and PFMERGE combines several into one, and a write or read takes constant time and space [[redis-hll]]. Google's paper on running HyperLogLog in practice describes improvements that cut its memory and raise its accuracy for an important range of cardinalities, and notes that the algorithm parallelizes perfectly and computes its estimate in one pass [[hll-practice]].

For frequencies, the count-min sketch paper introduces a data structure of sublinear space for summarizing data streams. It allows point, range and inner-product queries to be answered approximately and quickly, with accuracy set by two parameters the user chooses [[cm-paper]].

stages.name: Going deeper
body: The main dial is bits per key. RocksDB says about 10 bits per key works well for many workloads and that the setting is continuously configurable from 1 to 20 or more. It warns about diminishing returns: 4.9 bits per key gives a 10% false positive rate and is 90% as effective as 100 bits, 9.9 bits gives 1%, and 15.5 bits gives 0.1% [[rocks-bloom]].

Sizing for growth is harder. Redis says to give a filter the number of items you expect: oversize it and you waste memory, undersize it and a new sub-filter is stacked on top. Adds stay equally fast but presence checks get slower, because each stacked filter is checked in turn. The default expansion is 2 [[redis-bloom]]. With NONSCALING, the error rate rises once the capacity is reached [[redis-bloom]].

RocksDB also documents the Ribbon filter, a Bloom alternative available as a drop-in since version 6.15.0. It saves about 30% of Bloom filter space but uses about 3-4x as much CPU on filters, mostly in the background jobs that build them, which the page calls usually a good trade because SST filters commonly use about 10% of system RAM and well under 1% of CPU [[rocks-bloom]].

terms.definition: Each extra bit per key lowers the false positive rate by less than the one before.
Adding a new Bloom filter on top of a full one so adds keep working, at the cost of slower checks.
A Bloom alternative that uses less space and more CPU, built from a fixed set of keys.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: In a real LSM-tree the filter belongs to the file. RocksDB builds a filter inside every sorted file, and when two files are merged it builds a new filter from scratch for the new file, so bits per key and the false positive rate stay predictable [[rocks-bloom]]. The page also lists statistics for the observed false positive rate, so you can measure whether a setting works [[rocks-bloom]].

Choosing is about cost on each side. A filter is worth it when the guarded step is much more expensive than the filter check, and when absent keys are common. For counts, a HyperLogLog suits a number that may be off by a few percent, such as unique visitors, because it stays small and merges. Redis lists unique visits to a page as the example, with one sketch per page per period [[redis-hll]].
Count-min sketches fit when you need how often, not how many. The paper frames accuracy as a pair of user-chosen parameters, so the sketch size follows the error you accept [[cm-paper]].

misconceptions.myth: A Bloom filter can tell you a key is definitely present.
misconceptions.truth: It can only guarantee absence. A positive answer is an estimate, and one in N positive answers will be wrong [[redis-bloom]].

misconceptions.myth: A bigger Bloom filter always pays for itself.
misconceptions.truth: RocksDB lists diminishing returns: 9.9 bits per key already gives a 1% false positive rate, and raising it to 15.5 bits only gets to 0.1% [[rocks-bloom]].

misconceptions.myth: A probabilistic count is too unreliable to use.
misconceptions.truth: Redis lists unique page visits as a standard use for a HyperLogLog, where a small error is fine and the sketch stays small [[redis-hll]].
